title: Faith as trust
hookLine: the Greek word pistis means trust, faithfulness, loyalty

cards: "Master, master, we perish." A small boat filling with water, a storm of wind come down on the lake, and men shouting. Jesus is asleep in the boat.
They wake him. He rebukes the wind and the waves, and there is a calm. Then he turns to his friends with one short question: "Where is your faith?"
He doesn't ask what they believe about him. They'd just called him master. He asks where their faith went when the water came in.

teach.b: The New Testament's word for faith is pistis, and in Greek it's a wide word: trust, faithfulness, and loyalty, the kind you keep to a friend.
So when the Gospels talk about faith, they don't only mean holding a list of ideas to be true. They mean leaning your weight on someone. That's why the question in the boat lands so hard.

The disciples ran to him for help; what they couldn't do, with the boat filling, was trust him. Luke even says that afterward they asked one another what manner of man this was. They were still working out who he was.
The Letter to the Hebrews pictures faith as nearly all trust.
Abraham is called, and "he went out, not knowing whither he went." No map, just a voice.

teach.h: LEAN NOT UNTO THINE OWN UNDERSTANDING.
teach.b: Proverbs puts it plainly: "Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding." Churches describe faith in different ways. Martin Luther stressed faith as trust in God's promise.
Catholic teaching speaks of a personal clinging to God, and also the mind's assent to what God has revealed. Orthodox writers describe a living relationship. Each holds trust in it somewhere.
And trust can live beside doubt.

teach.h: I BELIEVE; HELP THOU MINE UNBELIEF.
teach.b: In Mark's Gospel a father with a sick son says in one breath: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." And Jesus heals his son. Trust doesn't mean the storm is gone.
It means you're still in the boat, with your weight on someone.

how: Christians speak of faith as trusting God in daily life, and some bring their worries to God in prayer, alone or by asking others in their church to pray with them.

o: agreeing to a list of ideas without any doubts
a feeling of certainty that the storm will pass
leaning your weight on someone, not only holding ideas

games.q: faith as trust — tap the pairs.
p: a father with a sick son

s: in the boat, Jesus asks the disciples what they believe about him
he asks, where is your faith? they'd called him master; what failed was trust.
the Greek word pistis can mean faithfulness and loyalty as well as faith
it covers trust, faithfulness and loyalty.
Hebrews says Abraham knew where he was going when he set out
"he went out, not knowing whither he went." no map: just a voice, and his feet.

games.q: you're one of the disciples. the boat is filling with water and Jesus is asleep. what do you do?
o: wake him, shouting that you're perishing.
keep bailing and let him sleep.
games.why: they wake him: master, master, we perish. he calms the storm, then asks them, where is your faith?

practice: Notice where you're holding your own weight, your shoulders, your jaw, your hands, and let the chair or the floor take it; that's a small trust already.
Then bring to mind one person you could lean on a little more: someone to ask for help, to tell something true, or to hand a job you've been gripping.
If you pray, you can rest on the proverb's line, trust in the LORD with all thine heart; if you don't, just let the floor hold you.

wordCard.voice: Faith as trust. Pistis: not only believing something is true, but leaning your weight on someone, even in a storm, even with doubt beside it.

orig.note: Greek: faith, trust, faithfulness, loyalty — the New Testament's word for faith.

carryVoice: Your line: faith is trust. Even with doubt sitting right beside it. Go gently.
